newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Investor revolt threatens QNI-Gencor nickel merger.
newsitem.headline: Investor revolt threatens QNI-Gencor nickel merger.

text.p: Australian investors angry at what they see as an unfair deal to merge nickel producer QNI Ltd with Gencor Ltd's nickel division could scuttle the A$2.3 billion deal at a shareholders meeting, analysts said on Friday.

"We came back from their presentation here in Brisbane thinking this is a fantastic deal for Gencor and not good for QNI," said Nick Atkinson, an institutional dealer at Brisbane brokerage Wilson HTM.
"I don't think it will be passed by the shareholders," Atkinson said, adding that QNI may have paid up to three times too much for Gencor's Cerro Matoso nickel mine in Columbia.
"QNI are giving up control of the company for what could be considered at best fair value and they're getting no premium for control," one analyst said.
"I don't think it's going to get through the shareholder meeting," he added.

QNI and the South African-based mining group announced on Wednesday a proposal to merge their nickel operations, with Gencor eventually taking a 56 percent controlling interest in a new enlarged QNI that they said would be worth A$2.3 billion (US$1.73 billion).

The initial reaction was positive as shareholders eyed the prospect of their company becoming the world's fourth largest nickel producer. But analysts views darkened as they assessed the value of Gencor's major nickel asset, the Cerro Matoso mine.

Gencor bought the 46.58 percent of the mine it did not already own from the Columbian government for US$165.8 million in February this year, valuing the complete mine at US$355.95 million or A$475 million.
Gencor's other nickel assets are generally valued by analysts at around A$100 million, putting Gencor's contribution to the merged group at around $575 million.
Analysts have compared this A$575 million valuation with QNI's A$1.1 billion market capitalisation and wondered why QNI shareholders were getting only 44 percent of the enlarged group.
The increasing investor anger was evident in a clearly hostile briefing for analysts and investors, where QNI was forced to urge them not to reject the merger plan.
"I think it would be a tragedy if we didn't grab this opportunity. Shareholders would be making one hell of a big mistake," QNI managing director Wyn Davies told the briefing.
Davies rejected the valuation of Cerro Matoso using the sale of the Columbian government stake in February, saying the mine's planned expansion and low costs meant it was worth much more.

He said he could not divulge the valuation QNI used in its negotiations with Gencor, except to say Gencor had valued the mine at A$1.3 billion to A$1.8 billion when it recently considered whether it would sell the mine seperately.
Davies also warned that Gencor was not bluffing and would not return with a new takeover bid if the merger was rejected.
Analysts were also disappointed the merger would initially dilute earnings per share (EPS) because of high depreciation and amortisation costs.
A QNI official confirmed that EPS would be diluted by about 20 percent in the first year, but that the merger would produce strong EPS growth in the merged group's third and fourth years.
QNI's shares closed down nine cents at A$2.55, well below the A$2.85 reached just after the deal's announcement.
